articles.title: Closed-head injury produces a delayed, region-specific defect in glucose-carbon routing at the pyruvate branchpoint in APP/PS1 KI mice
articles.content: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD), and both conditions are associated with impaired glucose metabolism and mitochondrial dysfunction. We previously reported time-dependent mitochondrial dysfunction following closed-head injury (CHI) in amyloid precursor protein/presenilin 1 (APP/PS1) knock-in (KI) mice, but whether glucose-derived carbon labeling showed a corresponding temporal pattern remained unknown. We hypothesized that early deficits would involve tricarboxylic acid (TCA)-cycle metabolites, whereas chronic changes persisted upstream at the pyruvate-lactate branchpoint. Here, oral uniformly 13C-labeled glucose ([U-13C]-glucose) tracing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS)-based isotopologue analysis were used to quantify first-turn glucose-derived carbon fate in cortex and hippocampus. To distinguish the effects of age at injury from those of post-injury interval, mice were analyzed 1 month after injury either at 7 or 12 months of age or 8 months after injury at 12 months of age. The most pronounced alterations occurred 8 months after CHI, when KI mice exhibited increased pyruvate and lactate labeling in the cortex and broader increases in glycolytic labeling in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that in APP/PS1 KI mice, chronic closed-head injury produced a delayed shift in glucose-derived carbon labeling centered on glycolytic and pyruvate/lactate nodes, with loss of hippocampal precursor-product coupling but without broad reduction of first-turn TCA-linked labeling.

articles.title: Hormonal factors are poor indicators of endometriosis pain
articles.content: Endometriosis is a common yet understudied condition in which sex hormones play a key role in the etiology and pathophysiology of the disease. Sex hormones are dysregulated in endometriosis and are pharmacologically targeted to reduce symptoms including pain, but the relationships between endometriosis-related pain with sex hormone levels and their receptors are not clear. In 60 women previously diagnosed or undergoing laparoscopic surgery for the diagnosis of endometriosis, we collected patient-reported endometriosis/pelvic pain intensity in the last 30 days, pain interference scale, and the Endometriosis Health Profile 30 (EHP30) pain subscale. In a sub-sample of 38 participants, biopsies from control non-lesion pelvic peritoneum and endometrial lesion tissues were collected during surgery to analyze the tissue abundance of the primary receptors for estrogen, as well as androgen, progesterone, and prolactin receptors. Serum was collected to analyze systemic sex hormone levels including estradiol, prolactin, progesterone, and testosterone. Between tissues, we found elevated transcript levels for estrogen receptor alpha (ESR1) in lesions, but no difference in estrogen receptor beta (ESR2) transcript levels between tissue samples were found. Relating tissue receptor transcript levels to clinical pain revealed that only ESR1 and PGR in lesions were negatively associated with endometriosis/pelvic pain intensity, however, following false discovery rate correction the association with ESR1 was no longer statistically significant. No other tissue or systemic factors were associated with clinical pain outcomes. Together, these data demonstrate unique alterations in receptor abundance in lesions yet select transcript levels only weakly relate to pain in endometriosis.

articles.title: The potato cyst nematode Globodera pallida possesses an expanded serotonergic nervous system
articles.content: Abstract The neurotransmitter serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; 5-HT) controls behaviours that are essential for the parasitic lifestyle of plant parasitic nematodes (PPNs). Here, we used serotonin immunochemistry and in situ hybridization for the serotonin synthesis genes, Gpa-tph-1 and Gpa-bas-1, to map its signalling pathways in Globodera pallida J2 infective stages. We identified fourteen serotonin-immunoreactive cell bodies around the pharyngeal median bulb and revealed that eleven of them co-express Gpa-tph-1 and Gpa-bas-1, confirming these are serotonin-synthesising neurons. Serotonin immunoreactivity was also localised in structures consistent with labelling of amphids, and in sixteen non-neuronal cells located in the middle and posterior region of the nematode. Depletion of serotonin with reserpine reduced the serotonin immunoreactivity in all fourteen cell bodies confirming their neuronal identity, but not in non-neuronal tissue. We identified additional, but infrequent expression of Gpa-tph-1 in two cells and expression of Gpa-bas-1 in one pair of symmetrically bilateral cells anterior to the median bulb, that lacked serotonin immunoreactivity. The results reveal distinct pools of serotonin distribution in G. pallida and indicate serotonin signalling is more complex than in other parasitic nematodes and C. elegans, highlighting evolutionary divergence in neurotransmitter identity.
articles.author: Coke, M. C., Lilley, C. J., Healey, R., O'Connor, V. M., Holden-Dye, L. M., Urwin, P. E.

articles.title: SAIL: Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretable Alignment of Human Vision and Multimodal Large Language Models
articles.content: Alignment between human high-level visual representations and those of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offers a quantitative framework for understanding information processing in human vision. However, similarities between model and brain representations do not directly reveal the semantic content underlying their correspondence, as this content is difficult to isolate in entangled MLLM representations. Here, we introduce SAIL, an interpretable framework that formulates voxel interpretation as a multi-unit sparse semantic correspondence problem between MLLMs and human vision. First, we train unified cross-layer sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on MLLM representations of Natural Scenes Dataset images and captions, and align each brain voxel with multiple SAE units. Second, we quantify semantic similarity between their top-response image sets to map semantic alignment across the cortex. We project multiple semantic labels back onto the cortex to interpret the content of this alignment. Finally, we assess these correspondences using category responses measured in independent fLoc experiments. Compared with SAEs trained independently at each layer, SAIL exhibits lower redundancy in SAE unit response profiles and higher semantic alignment. We find that semantic alignment is organized along the human ventral visual pathway across the models and subjects examined. The projected labels reveal semantic preferences within canonical visual regions, while fLoc experiments show agreement between predicted and measured category response patterns. Exploratory analyses further reveal cortical distributions of action-related semantics consistent with established functional accounts of lateral occipitotemporal and posterior parietal cortex. Overall, SAIL provides an interpretable account of the semantic correspondences between MLLM representations and human visual responses.
articles.author: Gao, T., Zhang, L., Wang, Y., Wang, Y., Zhou, H., Xue, M., Yang, G.

articles.title: Netrin signaling shapes sexually dimorphic neurite branching of a sex-shared interneuron in C. elegans
articles.content: Sexually dimorphic behaviors arise from underlying differences in neural circuit architecture between the sexes, yet the molecular mechanisms that establish these structural differences remain poorly understood. In Caenorhabditis elegans, the sex-shared interneuron AVG exhibits sexually dimorphic synaptic connectivity, offering a model for investigating the development of sexually dimorphic neuronal morphology. Here, we identified that AVG displays male-specific neurite branching and demonstrated that the conserved axon guidance cue UNC-6/Netrin and its receptor UNC-40/DCC are essential for this structural remodeling. Cell-specific manipulation of sexual identity revealed that male identity confers branching competence to AVG. Loss of UNC-6 or UNC-40 abolished branch formation, whereas loss of the alternate Netrin receptor UNC-5/Unc5 had no detectable effect. Cell-specific rescue experiments showed that UNC-40 functions in AVG through its UNC-6 binding domains. Furthermore, genetic ablation of the male-specific presynaptic neuron PCA, which expresses unc-6, diminished AVG branch length, establishing PCA as a candidate local source of UNC-6. Together, our findings support a model in which presynaptic UNC-6/Netrin cues from male-specific neurons promote dimorphic neurite branching in sex-shared neurons, illustrating how evolutionarily conserved signaling molecules are redeployed during sexual maturation to sculpt sex-specific neural circuits.
articles.author: Kang, D.-H., Kim, D., Park, G., Kim, B.

articles.title: On-demand surround suppression explains the spatiotemporal window of the tilt illusion
articles.content: What we see at one location depends on what surrounds it. Such contextual e[ff]ects are thought to arise from neural signals that travel across the retinotopic representations.Because these signals need more time to travel longer distances, a more distant surround should influence perception most strongly when presented earlier, compensating for its delay. We tested this prediction in human observers using a visual illusion in which a central target appears tilted away from the orientation of its surround (tilt illusion). Measuring the temporal window of this illusion using psychophysical reverse correlation revealed the opposite: the most e[ff]ective surround occurred progressively later as distance increased. Computational modelling demonstrated that this reversal is explained if the visual system sends out a query that recruits contextual information on demand. Perceptual appearance may thus be constructed through temporally unfolding interactions in which context is actively gathered, not passively received.
articles.author: Nakamura, T., Okubo, L., Miyoshi, K., Murakami, I.

articles.title: Facial color properties affect perceived age.
articles.content: Age is a fundamental social attribute that affects rights, responsibilities and even social status. Color information of the face can affect perceived age, but the nature of its contribution, independent of luminance information, remains underexplored. To better characterize the role of color in age perception, we conducted two experiments. In our first experiment, we tested whether natural age-related changes in facial color alone can drive changes in perceived age. In our second experiment, we manipulated red-green contrast across faces aged 18-91 and tested the effect of this manipulation of perceived youthfulness. Our findings demonstrate that natural age-related color changes do provide cues for age perception, dissociable from luminance information. We also found that the optimal red-green contrast level to make faces look the youngest was significantly higher than the originals, meaning that faces tended to appear younger when their redness was accentuated, even though average face redness increases with age. Our analysis revealed that younger faces required greater increases in redness level compared to their older counterparts to achieve the youngest appearance. These results suggest that the spatial distribution of redness contributes to apparent youthfulness, especially in younger faces.
articles.author: Hsieh, J., Clifford, C. W. G., Goddard, E.

articles.title: Resolution-aware spectral parameterization reveals robust context-dependent aperiodic EEG dynamics during real-world table tennis
articles.content: Mobile EEG can link neuroimaging to natural behavior, but effects recorded during movement, and sport in particular, are difficult to interpret because neural activity overlaps with signals from movement, muscle activity, and cable movement artifacts. We analyzed the OpenNeuro Real World Table Tennis dataset to test whether peri-hit spectral activity could be analyzed and how it differed between human-opponent and ball-machine play. Data from 25 participants comprising EEG, noise-layers, EMG and motion recordings was analyzed with pre-hit, impact, and post-hit windows. EEG power bands were residualized using trial-level root mean square from noise-layer, EMG, and motion/miscellaneous channels. Spectral parameterization modeled spectra as an aperiodic component plus periodic peaks. The principal short-window model was resolution-aware; sensitivity analyses reduced model complexity, used a 2.0-s peri-hit subwindow (-1.0 to +1.0 s), or disabled periodic fitting. Results showed residualized alpha and beta power was lower during ball-machine play, including pre-hit posterior alpha power. The clearest context difference was a higher ball-machine aperiodic exponent over posterior and parietal sensors, corresponding to a steeper broadband spectral slope. Posterior post-hit means were 0.451 and 0.606 for human-opponent and ball-machine play, respectively. A focal parietal effect persisted across specifications. The results support artifact-informed, resolution-aware spectral analysis as an effective approach for detecting robust spectral differences between naturalistic visuomotor contexts and suggest that EEG may provide useful information about the processes engaged by different practice environments, without establishing a single cognitive or physiological mechanism or demonstrating a training outcome.
articles.author: Guchait, A., Chen, C.-Y., Muggleton, N. G.

articles.title: A comprehensive physiological dataset of pain and aversive modalities for pain biomarkers research
articles.content: While progress has been made in identifying pain biomarkers using neuroimaging, the development of reliable EEG-based biomarkers remains challenging, limited by small sample sizes and the lack of adequate control conditions. We present a comprehensive dataset from 125 pain-free adults, comprising electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings, and behavioural, sociodemographic, and psychological data. Galvanic skin response and electrocardiogram data were also recorded in a subset of participants (n = 76). Participants received two sustained painful stimulations (thermal, chemical) and two sustained aversive non-painful stimulations (auditory, taste), each delivered twice (with and without continuous intensity ratings). Data are provided in Brain Imaging Data Structure format, where all physiological, stimulus-related, and behavioural data are synchronized within the EEG data files for easy access and analysis. Technical validation confirmed data integrity, with spectral and physiological analyses showing responses associated with stimulus intensity and subjective pain/unpleasantness levels. By providing multimodal physiological data across painful and non-painful aversive conditions, this initiative represents a valuable resource for developing or validating biomarkers and exploring the multidimensional nature of pain perception.
articles.author: Champagne, A., Barrette, L.-E., Cyr-Bouchard, A., Roy, M., Coll, M.-P.

articles.title: Bone Marrow-Derived Cells Fuse with Bergmann Glia in Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis
articles.content: Bone marrow-derived cells (BMDCs) can infiltrate the brain and adopt new identities through transdifferentiation or fusion, yet their interactions with specific neural cells remain poorly defined. We examined BMDC fusion with Bergmann glia (BG), a key cerebellar support cell, in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis. After bone marrow transplantation, BMDCs fused with BG to form heterokaryons, retaining BG morphology and molecular markers. These heterokaryons contained donor and host nuclei that differed in both morphology and transcriptional activity. Remarkably, the BMDC nucleus localized not only to the soma but also along BG processes. This discovery identifies BMDC-BG fusion as a previously unrecognized form of glial plasticity, opening avenues for therapeutic strategies aimed at potentiating glial-mediated repair.

Threatening events and other themes in COVID-19-related dreams: Examining pandemic dreams from the perspective of current dream simulation theories.
articles.content: In this study on pandemic dream experiences in rural Nepal, 54 interviews were collected 1 year into the COVID-19 pandemic and compared with 62 interviews collected some years earlier. As in comparable studies, the dream narratives were categorized and analyzed according to their content, employing methods applied in other studies. The frequency of dream themes was matched with predictions derived from three current strands in dream research: (a) threat simulation theory (TST); (b) the incorporation continuity hypothesis (ICH); and (c) social simulation theory (SST). The pandemic sample contained more reported nightmares and both aggressive and nonaggressive threats than the nonpandemic sample (supporting TST). The pandemic sample also exhibited more reported dream events associated with disease and illness than the nonpandemic sample (supporting ICH). There were both increased and decreased frequencies of social dream events between the two samples—weakly supporting and somewhat contradicting SST. An additional aim of the study was to relate the reported dream experiences to purportedly cultural factors in dreaming. The three dream theories (TST, SST, ICH) are discussed in relation to the concept of dream simulation as input conditioned by, and/or output conditioning, cultural transmission. The frequently recurring supernatural and religious content of the dream narratives seem to suggest the viability of all three dream theories. This license permits copying and redistributing the work in any medium or format, as well as adapting the material for any purpose, even commercially.” https://doi.org/10.1037/drm0000349 (The following abstract of the original article appeared in record 2027-47158-001.) Dreams represent a universal human experience linked to emotional regulation, memory processing, and psychological well-being, yet the extent to which stable personality traits shape dream experiences remains unclear. Previous reviews have either focused narrowly on nightmares or examined general sleep-related patterns, leaving questions about the broader role of personality in dreaming unresolved. This meta-analytic investigation synthesized evidence from 89 studies across 86 articles (comprising 65,474 participants) to examine associations between the Big-Five personality traits and nocturnal dream phenomena, including general/neutral dreams, nightmares, and lucid dreams. Déjà rêvé, erotic dreams, and sleep paralysis were also included, though limited studies explored these phenomena precluding analyses into these domains. Neuroticism yielded consistent associations with nightmare frequency, intensity, distress, proneness, and with heightened emotional tone in general/neutral dreams. Openness was broadly linked to cognitive–perceptual engagement, encompassing greater dream recall, vividness, intensity, attitudes, sharing, and a weak positive association with lucid dreaming. Extraversion was narrowly related to socially expressive dimensions including dream sharing, whereas Agreeableness and Conscientiousness yielded inconsistent associations. These findings support continuity models in which affective vulnerability and cognitive–perceptual orientation shape dream experiences. They also emphasize the applied significance of dreaming as a meaningful psychological domain. Nightmares may provide accessible markers of affective dysregulation and potential intervention targets, whereas openness-related engagement with dreams may be harnessed as a resource for creativity, reflection, and well-being. By situating dreaming within the framework of personality research, this study advances theoretical understanding and highlights practical opportunities for integrating dream research into clinical and educational contexts. articles.title: When the body suffers, the mind dreams: The lived experience of cancer.
articles.content: Dreams have intrigued humanity across centuries, serving as portals to the unconscious, reflections of lived experiences, and sources of spiritual guidance. The study of dreaming spans neuroscience, psychology, anthropology, sociology, and religious thoughts, with each discipline offering unique insights into the meaning and function of dreams. For individuals facing life-threatening illnesses like cancer, dreaming can assume an intense significance. Dreams may reveal unresolved fears, induce the struggle for survival, or provide moments of transcendence and hope. This article explores the phenomenon of dreaming through both scholarly and personal lenses. As a cancer patient and researcher, I examine dreams not only as neurocognitive events but also as deeply affective and cultural phenomena. Drawing upon psychoanalytic theories, neuroscientific evidence, and cultural understandings of dreams, I situate my personal dream experiences within the broader research landscape. Using an autoethnographic approach, I reflect that how my dreams have shifted through the phases of diagnosis, treatment, prognosis, and recovery and how these dreams induced both anxiety and comfort. Ultimately, this exploration underscores the value of dreams as a psychological resource and an avenue for understanding the lived experience of cancer. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

articles.title: The dream insight framework: Harnessing the power of dreams in leadership.
articles.content: This article introduces the Dream Insight Framework, an approach for integrating dreamwork into leadership development. It explores how dreams, often dismissed in existing leadership approaches, can be powerful tools for enhancing creativity, decision-making, and problem-solving. By reviewing existing theories and research, the article argues for a deeper engagement with the unconscious mind, proposing practical methods for leaders to harness dream insights to navigate complex challenges and develop leadership skills and qualities.
